paragraphs: Generating a graph involves coordinating its connections with the features attached to its nodes. The score-based models studied here describe these two parts through dependent stochastic differential equations. Because the equations interact, convergence analyses developed for models governed by a single equation do not directly apply. The paper develops an analysis that explicitly handles this dependence.

The authors bound generative error in three settings: generating node features while keeping the graph fixed, generating graph structure while keeping features fixed, and generating both together. This separation clarifies how the generation task changes the analysis. Their results identify graph-specific influences on the error bound, including topological properties that describe how the graph is connected.

The analysis also provides guidance for choosing sampling steps and diffusion length, and supports normalization as a way to improve convergence. A controlled study using synthetic graphs checks the theoretical findings empirically. The contribution therefore connects mathematical understanding of coupled graph generation with practical choices involved in building and running these models.
icml-2025-a-non-asymptotic-convergent-an.tldr: The paper bounds error in score-based graph generation while accounting for dependencies between graph structure and node features.

paragraphs: Many selection problems require a small set of choices to serve several objectives at once. This paper studies a formulation that maximizes the lowest value among multiple submodular functions, subject to a limit on the number of selected items. Focusing on the weakest objective makes the formulation relevant to robust decisions and fairness, where a strong overall result can otherwise conceal poor outcomes for some objectives.

Existing polynomial-time approximation methods face a practical trade-off: they either provide weaker guarantees or depend on an expensive mathematical construction called the multilinear extension. The authors introduce an algorithm described as the first scalable, practical method to achieve the best-known approximation guarantee. Its importance lies in bringing that guarantee within reach of practical computation.

The paper also introduces fair centrality maximization and expresses it through this multiobjective framework. In the reported experiments, the proposed method improves both objective value and running time compared with known algorithms. These findings support its usefulness when balancing several objectives must remain computationally manageable.
icml-2025-an-asymptotically-optimal-appr.tldr: A practical algorithm achieves the best-known approximation guarantee for selecting a limited-size set that balances multiple submodular objectives.

paragraphs: Subgraph neural networks gain expressive power by processing collections of subgraphs rather than treating a graph only as a single object. Their computational burden grows because those collections typically expand with the number of nodes. HyMN addresses this bottleneck by choosing a small collection of relevant subgraphs, reducing the amount of material the network must process.

The selection uses walk-based centrality measures, which characterize structural importance through walks on the graph. The authors connect this sampling strategy to perturbation analysis to explain its strengths. They also prove that the same centrality measures can serve as structural encodings that improve discriminative power. Thus, the structural information helps both select subgraphs and enrich their representations.

Experiments show a useful balance of efficiency, expressiveness, and downstream performance, including application to substantially larger graphs. HyMN outperforms more elaborate subgraph sampling methods and is competitive with, sometimes better than, other leading approaches while using a fraction of their runtime. Those comparisons support selective processing as a practical route to scaling subgraph networks.
icml-2025-balancing-efficiency-and-expre.tldr: HyMN uses walk-based centrality to select fewer subgraphs and improve structural representations, making expressive graph networks more efficient.

paragraphs: Designing a molecule to interact with two proteins requires balancing several goals, including affinity for each target and desirable molecular properties. Combining these goals into one number can obscure meaningful trade-offs. The paper also identifies a separate weakness in existing approaches: synthetic planning is often absent from the process that generates candidate molecules.

CombiMOTS addresses both issues through Pareto Monte Carlo Tree Search. It explores a space of synthesizable molecular fragments while keeping target affinity and physicochemical requirements as a vector of objectives. This allows the search to represent competing goals explicitly, rather than reducing every comparison to a single combined score. Synthesis considerations are incorporated into the search space itself.

Experiments using real-world databases produce novel candidate molecules with high docking scores, greater diversity, and balanced pharmacological characteristics. These findings support the framework's potential for dual-target discovery. The reported evidence concerns generated candidates and their evaluated properties; the therapeutic efficiency, safety, and resistance benefits discussed in the motivation remain potential advantages of dual-target molecules.
icml-2025-combimots-combinatorial-multi-.tldr: CombiMOTS searches synthesizable molecular fragments while explicitly balancing affinity for two protein targets and other molecular properties.

paragraphs: A document question-answering system can return an answer without making clear which parts of the document justify it. DocVXQA aims to produce both an accurate answer and a visual explanation. Its heatmaps highlight important document regions so that a user can inspect the visual basis offered for the system's decision.

The central design choice is to make explanation quality part of learning. The authors translate explainability principles into explicit quantitative training criteria. Their approach goes beyond emphasizing regions associated with the answer: it seeks enough surrounding context to support the explanation while keeping the representation efficient. This balances the need to show supporting information with the need for a focused, interpretable explanation.

The paper reports extensive experiments, including human evaluation, that provide strong evidence for the method's effectiveness. Its contribution is therefore both a document-answering framework and a way to train for the quality of accompanying visual explanations. The stated goal is to balance predictive performance and interpretability while helping users understand and trust model decisions.
icml-2025-docvxqa-context-aware-visual-e.tldr: DocVXQA learns to answer document questions while highlighting compact, contextually sufficient visual evidence for its answers.

paragraphs: Data-driven weather models can perform strongly overall while producing forecasts that smooth away fine-scale structure. This paper links that smoothing to the mean squared error objective commonly used in training. Its double-penalty effect makes the loss function itself an obstacle to preserving detailed weather patterns, even when the forecasting model is otherwise capable.

The authors develop a simple modification that separates errors caused by decorrelation from errors in spectral amplitude. This distinguishes two sources of mismatch that the usual objective combines. The proposed loss introduces no additional parameters, giving the authors a direct way to change the training signal without adding a new set of loss parameters to tune.

Fine-tuning GraphCast with this objective produces sharper deterministic forecasts and increases its effective resolution from 1,250 kilometers to 160 kilometers. The reported benefits also include improved ensemble spread and better predictions of tropical cyclone strength and extreme surface winds. These results show that changing the objective can materially improve the detail and weather phenomena represented in this forecasting model.
icml-2025-fixing-the-double-penalty-in-d.tldr: A parameter-free loss modification gives GraphCast sharper forecasts and improves its effective resolution and predictions of weather extremes.

paragraphs: Equivariance describes how a model's outputs should change consistently when its inputs undergo a relevant transformation. Incorporating such structure into vector-valued Gaussian processes can require kernels whose evaluation integrates over transformation groups. Those integrations can be computationally expensive, making a mathematically appropriate model difficult to use in practice.

The paper develops a kernel characterization of stochastic equivariance for centered, second-order vector-valued random fields. It then constructs equivariant kernels that avoid the integrations, using fundamental regions of group actions. The result connects a theoretical description of the required symmetry with a construction intended to make kernel evaluation computationally lighter.

The authors establish data-efficient, lightweight Gaussian process models for velocity fields and molecular electric dipole moments. They also demonstrate that the kernels may be used to extract equivariant components from data. The contribution therefore supports both prediction with known transformation structure and analysis of data for components that follow that structure, extending beyond a single application of Gaussian process modeling.
icml-2025-integration-free-kernels-for-e.tldr: The paper constructs equivariant kernels without costly group integrations, enabling lightweight Gaussian process models for structured vector-valued data.

paragraphs: Ranking, sorting, and selecting the largest values are useful operations, but incorporating their behavior into gradient-based learning calls for differentiable versions. This paper introduces one technique for constructing several such operations: soft ranking, soft top-k selection, and soft permutations. A shared construction connects tasks that otherwise might require separate methods.

The method centers on LapSum, defined using a sum of Laplace distributions. The authors derive an efficient closed-form formula for its inverse and use it to build the differentiable operations. For selecting high activations, the approach has low computational and memory requirements, with losses and gradients computed in O(n log n) time for an input of size n.

Extensive experiments report better performance than leading techniques for high-dimensional vectors and large values of k. These are settings where efficient handling of many entries and large selections matters particularly. The authors also provide CPU and CUDA implementations, connecting the mathematical formulation to practical use in large-scale differentiable ordering and ranking problems.
icml-2025-lapsum-one-method-to-different.tldr: LapSum provides a shared, efficient construction for differentiable ranking, top-k selection, and permutations.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making with adversarial losses, stochastic constraints, and bandit feedback. The learner must improve its decisions while controlling constraint violations despite limited feedback. The analysis distinguishes three settings according to what is known about the existence of a policy that satisfies the constraints strictly.

For general constrained Markov decision processes, the authors obtain sublinear regret and sublinear cumulative positive constraint violation. If a strictly feasible policy exists and is known, another algorithm achieves sublinear regret while satisfying the constraints in every episode with high probability. If such a policy exists but is unknown, the authors instead obtain sublinear regret with constant cumulative positive violation. These are distinct guarantees, with stronger feasibility information enabling stronger control.

The paper also proves that dependence on Slater's parameter is unavoidable in the latter two settings. Its contribution is a theoretical treatment of adversarial losses together with hard constraints. The results clarify how available feasibility information shapes the guarantees possible in non-stationary environments.
icml-2025-learning-adversarial-mdps-with.tldr: The paper gives learning guarantees for adversarial decision processes with hard constraints, distinguishing whether a strictly feasible policy exists and is known.

paragraphs: A useful distance between data points can depend on where other data are concentrated. Density-based distances make travel through low-probability regions more costly, encouraging shortest paths to follow the data manifold. Fermat distances implement this idea, but existing nearest-neighbor graph estimators suffer from inaccurate density estimates and paths that are insufficiently smooth, particularly in high dimensions.

The authors replace key parts of that estimation process with learned models. Normalizing flows estimate the data density, and a learned score model guides a relaxation procedure that refines the paths. These components address two connected problems: understanding the distribution well enough to define meaningful travel costs, and finding smoother paths under those costs.

The paper also introduces a dimension-adapted Fermat distance designed to scale more intuitively as dimensionality increases and to improve numerical stability. Together, these changes aim to make density-based metric learning more practical in high-dimensional spaces. The contribution is an approach to learning both the underlying geometry and the paths used to measure distances within it.
icml-2025-learning-distances-from-data-w.tldr: Learned density and score models improve the estimation of distances whose shortest paths follow the data distribution.

paragraphs: Medical codes carry information through both their descriptions and their relationships to other codes. Treating each as an isolated textual token leaves out context such as hierarchical organization, disease co-occurrence, and drug-treatment associations. MedTok builds this information into the tokenization stage used by models trained on electronic health records.

A language model encoder processes code descriptions, while a graph encoder represents relational structure. MedTok then quantizes both into a shared discrete token space that preserves information specific to each modality and information connecting them. The approach changes how medical codes are represented before an EHR model uses them for prediction.

The authors integrate MedTok into five EHR models and evaluate operational and clinical tasks across inpatient and outpatient datasets. Replacing standard tokenizers improves AUPRC across all tested models, with reported gains of 4.10% on MIMIC-III, 4.78% on MIMIC-IV, and 11.32% on EHRShot. Drug recommendation shows the largest gains. An additional demonstration in medical question answering supports the tokenizer's potential beyond EHR prediction alone.
icml-2025-multimodal-medical-code-tokeni.tldr: MedTok combines medical-code descriptions and relationships into shared tokens, improving results across five evaluated EHR models.

paragraphs: Operator learning concerns learning mappings between functions. This paper asks how the choice of training data affects that process when the target operator is linear. Its analysis assumes that input functions come from a mean-zero stochastic process with a continuous covariance kernel, making the structure of variation in those functions central to the result.

For an active data collection strategy, the authors derive an error convergence rate governed by how quickly the covariance kernel's eigenvalues decay. Under sufficiently rapid decay, the active strategy can achieve arbitrarily fast error convergence. The conditional nature of this result matters: the speed comes from combining active collection with favorable covariance structure.

The paper contrasts this with passive, independently sampled data, whose convergence is described as no faster than inverse sample size. It further establishes a non-vanishing lower bound for passive collection in the studied setting, regardless of eigenvalue decay. These results show that selecting data actively can offer substantial theoretical advantages under the paper's operator and input assumptions.
icml-2025-on-the-benefits-of-active-data.tldr: For the studied linear operators, active data collection can achieve arbitrarily fast convergence when covariance eigenvalues decay sufficiently rapidly.

paragraphs: The performance of a graph neural network depends on both the graph and the algorithm used to learn from it. This paper studies that relationship in a setting with noise, focusing on generalization through excess risk. It moves beyond analyses centered on noise-free fitting and coarse graph summaries such as maximum degree.

The authors derive excess-risk profiles for stochastic gradient descent and Ridge regression, then connect those profiles to graph structure using spectral graph theory. This provides a framework for comparing how regular and power-law graphs affect the two learning algorithms. The focus is on how structural properties shape learning performance, rather than only how quickly an algorithm converges.

The analysis extends to multilayer linear GNNs, where it reveals an increasingly direction-dependent effect on excess risk. This gives a learning-algorithm perspective on over-smoothing. Empirical results agree with the theoretical predictions, supporting the view that graph structure, network design, and learning algorithm should be considered together when choosing or developing a GNN.
icml-2025-on-the-interplay-between-graph.tldr: The paper connects graph structure to the generalization behavior of SGD and Ridge regression in GNNs through spectral analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making when the learner must obey a safety rule it does not initially know. The objective combines two demands: keep each round’s action safe with high probability, and achieve low regret relative to the best safe action chosen with hindsight. This makes learning the safety rule part of the decision problem itself.

The authors propose a general method that connects two learning components. An online regression oracle estimates the unknown constraint, while an online learning oracle proposes decisions. The method transforms those proposals into decisions that satisfy the safety requirement. This structure lets constraint estimation and decision-making contribute separately to the overall guarantee.

The regret bound depends on both oracles’ regret, the eluder dimension of the model class containing the true constraint, and a new measure of how difficult safe learning is. An asymptotic lower bound shows that this new complexity measure is necessary, giving it significance beyond its appearance in the proposed method’s analysis.

For linear constraints, the authors obtain a concrete algorithm with regret growing as the square root of the number of rounds. Its scaling transformation balances optimistic exploration with pessimistic constraint satisfaction: exploration supports learning, while caution supports safety. The result establishes that, in this setting, regret can grow more slowly than the interaction length while maintaining the stated safety guarantee.
icml-2025-online-learning-with-unknown-c.tldr: The paper develops a general method for learning under unknown safety constraints, with per-round high-probability safety and square-root regret for linear constraints.

paragraphs: More pre-training is often expected to produce a better starting point for downstream adaptation. This paper shows that extending pre-training can instead make a language model harder to fine-tune and reduce its final performance. The authors call this phenomenon catastrophic overtraining, emphasizing that pre-training progress and adaptability do not always improve together.

One reported example compares instruction-tuned OLMo-1B models pre-trained on different token budgets. The version trained on 3 trillion tokens performs over 2% worse on multiple standard language-model benchmarks than the version trained on 2.3 trillion tokens. This illustrates the phenomenon through downstream results rather than assuming that a stronger pre-training outcome guarantees a better adapted model.

Controlled experiments and theoretical analysis connect the effect to a systematic increase in the sensitivity of pre-trained parameters to modification. That sensitivity extends beyond fine-tuning itself. The findings motivate evaluating pre-training choices partly through how well the resulting parameters tolerate later adaptation, since downstream usefulness can depend on both what a model learns and how readily it can change.
icml-2025-overtrained-language-models-ar.tldr: Extended pre-training can increase parameter sensitivity and make subsequent fine-tuning produce worse results.

paragraphs: PaperBench measures whether AI agents can carry out the work needed to replicate research, from understanding a paper to building code and executing experiments. Its tasks cover 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers. This makes the benchmark an assessment of sustained research engineering across several stages of a project.

The authors work with the original paper authors to create hierarchical grading rubrics, dividing the replications into 8,316 individually assessable tasks. That structure makes partial progress measurable through explicit criteria. They also develop an LLM judge for automated grading and a separate benchmark to assess how well such judges perform.

Among the evaluated agents, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with open-source scaffolding achieves the highest average replication score, 21.0%. Top machine-learning PhD researchers attempt a subset of the benchmark, and the tested models do not outperform that human baseline. The findings establish a concrete evaluation of current research-replication capabilities, while the released code supports further study of how those capabilities develop.
icml-2025-paperbench-evaluating-ais-abil.tldr: PaperBench evaluates end-to-end AI research replication, with the best tested agent achieving a 21.0% average replication score.

paragraphs: PDE-Controller connects natural-language instructions to control problems governed by partial differential equations. The challenge is to turn an informal request into a precise mathematical specification and then reason about how to act on it. The paper targets applied mathematical reasoning, where producing plausible language alone is insufficient for useful control.

The framework combines autoformalization, reasoning, and planning with resources designed for this task. These include human-written cases, two million synthetic samples, mathematical reasoning models, and evaluation metrics. By addressing data, models, and evaluation together, the authors build a pipeline for translating instructions into formal representations and using those representations to improve PDE control.

The reported evaluations show substantial improvements over the compared open-source and GPT models in reasoning, autoformalization, and program synthesis. PDE control utility gains improve by up to 62%. This maximum reported improvement supports the framework's potential for scientific and engineering control tasks, while the broader contribution is a concrete connection between language-based interaction and systems described by mathematical equations.
icml-2025-pde-controller-llms-for-autofo.tldr: PDE-Controller translates informal instructions into formal PDE control tasks and reports up to a 62% improvement in utility gain.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained sequential decision-making when rewards and constraints may be stochastic or adversarial. A useful algorithm should handle both kinds of environment without requiring a different approach for each. Earlier work provided such guarantees under full feedback, but relied on costly optimization over occupancy measures.

The authors introduce a best-of-both-worlds algorithm that operates with bandit feedback, where observations are limited to the consequences of chosen actions. It uses policy optimization, which the paper describes as substantially more efficient than occupancy-measure methods. This addresses both the information requirement and the computational burden of the earlier approach.

The guarantees differ by constraint setting. For stochastic constraints, regret and constraint violation grow on the order of square root of T, up to logarithmic factors. For adversarial constraints, violation has the same order while reward reaches a tight fraction of the optimum. Keeping these outcomes distinct matters: the contribution is one algorithm with appropriate guarantees for both settings, rather than an identical reward guarantee in each.
icml-2025-policy-optimization-for-cmdps-.tldr: A policy-optimization algorithm handles stochastic and adversarial constraints under bandit feedback, with setting-specific theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Missing values create a prediction problem and an interpretation problem: a model may depend on information that is unavailable or has been filled in artificially. Common responses, such as imputation and missingness indicators, can introduce bias or additional complexity. This paper trains models to reduce how often their predictions require missing or imputed feature values.

The missingness-avoiding framework adds model-specific regularization terms to training objectives. The authors develop versions for decision trees, tree ensembles, and sparse linear models. For tree-based models, the approach also uses contextual missingness, reducing reliance on unavailable values according to the observed context rather than treating a feature's availability as context-independent.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that MA-DT, MA-LASSO, MA-RF, and MA-GBT reduce reliance on features with missing values while retaining predictive performance competitive with their unregularized counterparts. The aim is to make predictions depend more directly on observed information. The reported results support this as a practical way to preserve interpretability when test-time data are incomplete.
icml-2025-prediction-models-that-learn-t.tldr: Missingness-avoiding training reduces dependence on unavailable feature values while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

paragraphs: Combinatorial auctions let bidders express preferences over bundles, but the number of possible bundles grows exponentially with the number of items. Learning useful preferences with few questions is therefore central to efficient auction design. The paper addresses a mismatch between machine-learning approaches that use value queries and practical auctions that use demand queries.

The authors introduce a learning algorithm that provably uses the full information available from both query types. Experiments show that combining them improves learning performance. They then build MLHCA, an auction that incorporates both forms of preference elicitation, using the complementary information to guide the allocation process.

In the reported experiments, MLHCA reduces efficiency loss by up to a factor of ten relative to the previous state of the art, while requiring up to 58% fewer queries. These are maximum reported gains, rather than uniform improvements for every case. The findings connect allocation efficiency with practical participation: asking fewer questions also reduces the cognitive work required from bidders.
icml-2025-prices-bids-values-one-ml-powe.tldr: MLHCA combines value and demand queries to improve auction efficiency while asking bidders fewer questions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs repeated feedback about how well actions perform. When evaluating that reward is expensive, the feedback calculation can make training prohibitively slow. AdaReMo addresses this bottleneck by approximating a complicated reward function with multiple localized neural models that can provide reward estimates quickly.

These approximations adapt as the agent's policy changes. Each model fits the currently explored part of the system using recent trajectories, keeping its focus aligned with the decisions the agent is actually making. This adaptation is central to the approach: the reward approximation follows the evolving training process rather than remaining fixed while the policy moves into different regions.

Across molecular generation, epidemic control, and spatial planning, the authors report more than a thousandfold speedup and a 14.6% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. The empirical findings indicate that faster reward evaluation can accompany improved outcomes in these expensive-to-evaluate systems. The contribution is a way to concentrate reward-modeling effort where the current policy needs it while reducing computational overhead.
icml-2025-reinforcement-learning-with-ad.tldr: AdaReMo adapts localized reward models to an evolving policy, reporting over 1,000-fold speedup across three expensive-to-evaluate systems.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion models face two connected obstacles: storing whole graphs demands substantial memory, and generating graph sizes different from those seen during training can be difficult. SBGD changes the representation used for generation to address both. It works in a block graph space that incorporates structural priors drawn from patterns in real-world graphs.

This representation reduces memory complexity by organizing graph structure into blocks. It also aims to capture fundamental structural patterns that can support generation at different sizes. The method therefore treats representation as a central part of scaling: how the graph is organized affects both computational requirements and the model's ability to transfer across graph sizes.

Experiments report memory improvements of up to sixfold while preserving comparable or sometimes better generation performance than leading methods. They also show improved generalization to unseen graph sizes. Beyond these results, the paper presents block-based generation as an example of modularization, where decomposing a complex generation task into manageable components opens a route to more scalable models.
icml-2025-sbgd-improving-graph-diffusion.tldr: SBGD generates graphs through a block representation, reducing memory use and improving generalization to unseen graph sizes.

paragraphs: Some visual questions require both an image and outside knowledge. Models must learn to integrate that added context, yet vision-language models are not inherently designed for this form of generation. SKVQA addresses the training-data gap with a synthetic multimodal dataset containing more than two million visual question-answer pairs linked to external knowledge sources.

Compared with previous datasets, SKVQA contains eleven times as many unique questions, covers more diverse domains, and draws from a broader range of image sources. Human evaluations support the quality of the generated pairs and the relevance of their associated context. The dataset is designed to exercise the connection between visual information, supplied knowledge, and the final answer.

Experiments show two uses: SKVQA is a challenging benchmark for knowledge-based visual question answering and an effective resource for adapting generative multimodal models. Models trained on it show improved generalization in both context-aware visual question answering and multimodal retrieval-augmented generation. The findings support targeted synthetic data as a way to teach models to use additional knowledge.
icml-2025-sk-vqa-synthetic-knowledge-gen.tldr: SKVQA supplies over two million synthetic visual question-answer pairs with external knowledge to train and evaluate context-aware multimodal models.

paragraphs: Bayesian sampling methods need diagnostics that assess whether their samples match a desired posterior distribution. Familiar measures such as effective sample size are unsuitable for methods that retain asymptotic bias. Kernel Stein discrepancy offers an alternative, but its quadratic cost in sample count, dimensionality challenges, and tuning requirements can limit practical use.

The authors introduce polynomial Stein discrepancy and an associated goodness-of-fit test. Its theoretical guarantee is deliberately specific: for Gaussian targets, the test detects differences in the first r moments. It is not fully convergence-determining, so this moment-sensitive guarantee should not be read as establishing complete distributional convergence.

In several empirical examples, the test has greater power than competing methods at lower computational cost. The paper also demonstrates its use in choosing hyperparameters for Bayesian sampling algorithms more efficiently. Together, these results position the method as a computationally useful diagnostic with a clear theoretical focus on moment differences, rather than a universal certificate that a sampler has recovered the entire target distribution.
icml-2025-the-polynomial-stein-discrepan.tldr: Polynomial Stein discrepancy offers an efficient sample-quality test with guarantees for detecting moment differences in Gaussian targets.

paragraphs: Textual chains of thought include words that maintain readable prose as well as information needed for reasoning. Processing the resulting long traces consumes computation. This paper explores a hybrid representation that replaces part of the early reasoning with discrete latent tokens generated by a VQ-VAE, shortening the trace while retaining text elsewhere.

The authors study the representation in two settings: training a model from scratch on the Keys-Finding Maze problem and fine-tuning language models for logical and mathematical reasoning. For fine-tuning, the vocabulary expands to include the new latent tokens. A training procedure randomly mixes latent and text tokens, helping the models adapt to the unfamiliar representations.

The approach outperforms the compared baselines across several benchmarks, with reported gains of 4.2% on Math, 4.1% on GSM8K, and 13.3% on Fresh-Gaokao-Math-2023 for the respective tested Llama models. Reasoning traces become 17% shorter on average. These results support mixed latent-and-text representations as a way to improve measured reasoning performance while reducing trace length.
icml-2025-token-assorted-mixing-latent-a.tldr: Mixing discrete latent tokens with text shortens reasoning traces by 17% on average while improving results on the evaluated benchmarks.
